pl-l4d46c3-d1e115.summary: Asks how Cassiodorus called justice and mercy two things always joined in God's judgment, since God's justice and mercy are one thing, the divine essence; for God, to be merciful is to be mercy, and to be just is to be justice, and to be merciful is to be just, since these are said of God essentially, not denominatively. Why then does Scripture call some works of mercy, others of justice?
claims: God's justice and mercy are the divine essence.

pl-l4d46c3-d1e121.summary: Answers that such distinctions express not diversity of the underlying thing signified but variety of senses and effects in creatures: 'just' predicates the divine essence and shows him as distributor and judge of merits; 'merciful' the essence and him as liberator of the wretched; 'good' the essence and him as author of all goods; 'God' the essence and him as to be feared. So some works are called of mercy, others of justice, not because different powers produce them, but because some show him as judge and others as merciful, 'merciful' in nature and 'merciful one' in exhibition.
claims: Divine names signify one essence with different effects implied.
Works are called of mercy or justice by what they show of God.

pl-l4d46c3-d1e124.summary: Objects: how can some works show him just and others merciful, if to be just and to be merciful are the same for him? If said by the same reason, the work showing him just shows him merciful, and the reverse.

pl-l4d46c3-d1e128.summary: Answers that when God is called just and merciful, the same divine essence is signified and predicated, yet different things are understood: by this we understand him as merciful one and just judge.
claims: The same essence is signified with different understandings.

pl-l4d46c3-d1e131.summary: Cites Origen: all that is God's is Christ, his wisdom, strength, justice, holiness, prudence; though one in substance, it is named variously for diverse senses: wisdom signifies instructing in divine and human things, justice the distributor or judge of merits, prudence the teacher of good, bad, and indifferent things.
claims: One divine reality is named variously by its senses.

pl-l4d46c3.summary: Asks how Cassiodorus can call God's justice and mercy two things, since they are one, the divine essence, predicated essentially, not denominatively. Lombard answers that the distinction of works of mercy, justice, and goodness expresses not diversity in what is signified but diversity of senses and effects in creatures: 'just' predicates the divine essence and shows God as distributor of merits, 'merciful' the essence and him as liberator of the wretched. To the objection that if justice and mercy are the same, every work showing one shows the other, he answers that the same essence is signified with different connotations, as Origen says of Christ as wisdom, justice, and prudence.
claims: God's justice and mercy are one divine essence.
Works are distinguished as of mercy or justice by their effects in creatures.
Divine names signify one essence with different connotations.
